stories.headline: The Surfmen of Indian River
stories.hook: Between 1876 and 1915, the surfmen of the Indian River Life-Saving Station saved more than 400 sailors. Their station still stands in Delaware Seashore State Park.
stories.lede: Before there was a Coast Guard on this coast, there were surfmen.
stories.body:
Before there was a Coast Guard on this coast, there were surfmen. They served at life-saving stations along the shore, and one of their stations still stands at Delaware Seashore State Park: the Indian River Life-Saving Station.

A service built for shipwrecks

The original station was built in 1876 for the United States Life-Saving Service, a federal organization created to respond to the alarming number of shipwrecks along the nation's coasts. The Life-Saving Service is the precursor of today's U.S. Coast Guard.

A building that moved

The station did not stay where it was built. It first stood about 400 feet closer to the shore, and a sand dune began to form around it almost as soon as it was finished. In 1877 it was moved to the spot where it stands now.

What visitors see today is the station restored to its 1905 appearance, down to the diamond-shaped trim.

The work

The men who served there were local, and they were called surfmen. They manned the station through the stormy winter months. When they were not answering a wreck, they drilled on rescue techniques by day and walked the beaches at night, watching for ships in distress.

The record of that work is the reason the building is kept. Delaware State Parks credits the surfmen of Station Indian River Inlet with saving the lives of more than 400 sailors between 1876 and 1915.

The station now

The site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1976, and it is operated today as a maritime museum, part of Delaware Seashore State Park. It honors the surfmen and the rescues they made. The Delaware Public Archives has also marked the station with a state historical marker.

Delaware State Parks runs programs at the station through the year, including demonstrations of the rescue equipment the surfmen trained with. Program dates, museum hours and any admission are set by the park; check its current listings before you go.

Why it is worth the stop

Most of the coast's history is told through things that were built to last: forts, towers, lighthouses. The life-saving station is different. It is a building about a kind of work, done by people from nearby, in the worst weather of the year, for strangers whose ships had failed them. For a station whose dune once forced it to move, it has lasted well.

Sources: Delaware State Parks' Indian River Life Saving Station page (destateparks.com) for the 1876 construction, the Life-Saving Service, the 1877 move, the 1905 restoration, the surfmen's duties and the more than 400 sailors saved between 1876 and 1915; the Delaware Public Archives historical marker for the station; National Register listing as described by Delaware State Parks. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit the station for this story. Hours, programs and fees are the park's; check its current information.

stories.headline: The Fifth Bridge Over the Inlet
stories.hook: The cable-stayed bridge over Indian River Inlet opened in 2012. It replaced a line of earlier bridges the inlet itself kept wearing down.
stories.lede: The bridge most people now picture at Indian River Inlet is the newest of several.
stories.body:
The bridge most people now picture at Indian River Inlet, the one with the tall pylons and the blue cable housings, is the newest of several to cross the same water.

The bridges before

Bridges have spanned the inlet since 1934. New ones followed in 1940, 1952 and 1965, and a fifth span opened in 1976 as a twin to the 1965 bridge. The 1965 and 1976 bridges were steel girder bridges, and the inlet's current scoured around them, which is why they had to be replaced.

That is the inlet's nature. It is a channel of moving water between the Atlantic and Indian River Bay, and moving water wears away what is put in it.

The cable-stayed bridge

The current bridge is officially the Charles W. Cullen Bridge, and it is a cable-stayed design. It opened to traffic in 2012. It is about 2,600 feet long, with a 950-foot main span over the inlet. That span hangs from stay cables running to four pylons, each nearly 250 feet tall, and the cables are encased in 152 blue stay pipes, which give the bridge its color.

Putting the main span across the whole inlet is the point of the design. Earlier bridges stood in the water the current was working on. This one carries traffic over it.

A bridge that reports on itself

The less visible part of the bridge is a structural health monitoring system, installed while it was being built. University of Delaware engineers, who worked on the system, describe it as the first permanent long-term monitoring system installed during initial construction on a long-span, cable-supported bridge in the United States. Its sensors keep track of how the bridge behaves over time.

Seeing it

The bridge carries Route 1 between Dewey Beach and Bethany Beach, and the inlet below sits within Delaware Seashore State Park. Anyone driving the coast highway crosses it. The better view is from the park land on either side of the inlet, where the full line of the pylons and cables can be seen.

Sources: DelDOT's archived Indian River Inlet Bridge (Charles W. Cullen Bridge) project pages (deldot.gov) for the bridge's design, dimensions and opening; the University of Delaware Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering on the structural health monitoring system (ccee.udel.edu); the history of the earlier bridges and scour as summarized in those sources and corroborated by secondary references. Sources differ on the exact 2012 opening (January vs. May), so the story says 2012. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit for this story.

stories.headline: Five High Tides: The Storm of 1962
stories.hook: For three days in March 1962, a nor'easter sat off the Delaware coast through five high tides. It took seven lives in Delaware and reshaped the beach towns.
stories.lede: The storm started on a Tuesday and did not leave until Thursday.
stories.body:
The storm started on a Tuesday and did not leave until Thursday. Between Tuesday, March 6, and Thursday, March 8, 1962, a nor'easter ground slowly up the Atlantic coast and stayed over Delaware long enough to bring five high tides. It is remembered as one of the most destructive storms in the First State's recorded history.

What made it different

Coastal storms come and go with a tide or two. This one did not move on. Lasting through five high tides, it pushed the Atlantic onto the Delaware coast again and again, and each tide arrived on top of damage the last one had done.

What it cost

The storm claimed seven lives in Delaware and about 40 along the East Coast. Damage along Delaware's Atlantic and Delaware Bay coasts was estimated at $50 million at the time, which the Delaware Public Archives puts at roughly $465 million today.

The beach towns took it hardest. The boardwalks in Bethany Beach and Rehoboth Beach were pulverized. The bay shore was hit too: the archives' photographs show damage at Bowers Beach and Slaughter Beach as well as along the ocean.

The record

Much of what is known about the storm in Delaware is visual. The Delaware Public Archives has digitized and curated more than 500 photographs of it from state agencies. They cover Bowers Beach, Slaughter Beach, Rehoboth Beach, Dewey Beach, the Indian River Inlet, Bethany Beach, Fenwick Island, Oak Orchard and Massey's Landing in Millsboro. Most had not been released before.

The collection is free to browse online. It is the closest anyone now living can come to seeing the coast as it looked when the water went down.

Why it still matters

Sixty-four years on, the Storm of 1962 remains the benchmark the Delaware coast is measured against: a reminder of what a slow storm with a long fetch of high tides can do. The towns rebuilt. The photographs are the record of why the rebuilding was needed.

Sources: Delaware Public Archives, "Storm of 1962" digital archives collection (archives.delaware.gov), for the March 6–8 dates, the five high tides, the seven Delaware deaths and about 40 on the East Coast, the $50 million (about $465 million today) damage estimate, the boardwalk and structural destruction, and the photograph collection; University of Delaware UDaily coverage of the storm's anniversary. Figures for wave heights and house counts that appear in other accounts were not consistently sourced and are left out. Delaware Beach Finds' account is drawn entirely from these records.

stories.headline: The Northernmost Cypress Swamp
stories.hook: Trap Pond State Park holds the northernmost naturally occurring stand of baldcypress in the United States. Most of what stands there now grew back after the loggers left.
stories.lede: An hour inland from the beaches, in western Sussex County, is a cypress swamp at the very northern edge of where cypress swamps grow.
stories.body:
An hour's drive inland from the beaches, in western Sussex County, is a cypress swamp at the very edge of where cypress swamps grow. Trap Pond State Park holds the northernmost naturally occurring stand of baldcypress in the United States.

A tree worth cutting

Baldcypress was prized for its rot-resistant wood, and the cypress around Trap Pond was harvested extensively. The pond itself comes out of that history: the wetland was dammed to power a small sawmill, Trap Mills, which cut the harvested cypress into saleable timber.

The two state sources disagree on when the dam went in. One puts it in the late 1700s, the other in the late 1800s. What they agree on is the result. Most of the baldcypress at Trap Pond today is second-growth, trees that came back after the logging.

From farmland to park

After the logging ended, landowners enlarged the pond and installed drainage tiles to dry out the surrounding land for farming. In 1930 the federal government bought Trap Pond and the farmland around it and brought in the Civilian Conservation Corps to develop the area for recreation.

In 1951, when Delaware's legislature authorized its first three state parks, Trap Pond was one of them. The state park system is 75 years old this year.

What it is now

Trap Pond is one of the state's inland parks, a long way in character from the dunes and surf of Cape Henlopen or Delaware Seashore. It is a place of still water, and of trees standing in it. For a visitor from the coast, it is a reminder that Sussex County is more than its beaches.

Programs, rentals and hours are set by Delaware State Parks and change with the season; check the park's current information before you go.

Sources: Delaware State Parks' Trap Pond page (destateparks.com) for the northernmost naturally occurring baldcypress stand and the park's history; DNREC's Trap Pond watershed success story (dnrec.delaware.gov) for the sawmill, the drainage tiles, the 1930 federal purchase and the Civilian Conservation Corps; the two sources' different dates for the dam are reported as a disagreement. Delaware State Parks' "Our Story" for the 1951 founding of the park system. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit the park for this story.

stories.headline: The Bays Behind the Beaches
stories.hook: Rehoboth Bay, Indian River Bay and Little Assawoman Bay sit behind the barrier beaches. Congress called them an estuary of national significance in 1988.
stories.lede: Most visitors see Delaware's coast from the ocean side. Behind the beaches is a second coast.
stories.body:
Most visitors see Delaware's coast from the ocean side. Behind the beaches is a second coast: three shallow bays known together as Delaware's Inland Bays.

Three bays

The Inland Bays are Rehoboth Bay, Indian River Bay and Little Assawoman Bay. Little Assawoman, the smallest, is also the southernmost. Together with the land that drains into them, they make up the Inland Bays watershed.

They are an estuary, a place where fresh water from the land meets salt water from the sea. Indian River Inlet is where that exchange with the Atlantic happens.

A national designation

In 1988 Congress designated the Inland Bays an estuary of national significance. That designation is what makes their stewardship part of the National Estuary Program, a network of 28 estuaries around the country.

The Center for the Inland Bays

The Delaware Center for the Inland Bays was established by the Delaware General Assembly in 1994 as an independent nonprofit. Its creation came after some 20 years of public participation and investigation into the decline of water quality in the bays.

Its mission is to preserve, protect and restore the Inland Bays and their watershed. It does that through a Comprehensive Conservation and Management Plan that covers scientific study of the bays' health, water quality improvement, restoration of fish and wildlife habitat, and public education about what affects the watershed.

Seeing them

The Center manages the James Farm Ecological Preserve in Ocean View, on Indian River Bay, which was a recent Delaware Beach Finds Hidden Gem. The preserve is open sunrise to sundown year-round, and the Center runs public programs there and around the bays.

The simplest way to understand the bays is to see them after a day at the ocean. They are calmer, shallower and quieter, and they are as much a part of the coast as the surf.

Sources: Delaware Center for the Inland Bays, "About" (inlandbays.org), for the three bays, the 1988 congressional designation, the 28 National Estuary Programs, the 1994 founding by the General Assembly after 20 years of public participation, the mission and the Comprehensive Conservation and Management Plan; the Center's "Visit the Preserve" page for James Farm's sunrise-to-sundown hours. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit for this story; program dates are the Center's.

stories.headline: The Lighthouse That Fell Into the Sea
stories.hook: Cape Henlopen's lighthouse was lit in 1769, survived the Revolution and stood for more than a century and a half. On April 13, 1926, the eroding dune let it go.
stories.lede: For a century and a half, a lighthouse stood on the dunes at Cape Henlopen. Then the sand underneath it left.
stories.body:
For a century and a half, a lighthouse stood on the dunes at Cape Henlopen. Then the sand underneath it left.

A colonial light

The Cape Henlopen Lighthouse was completed in 1767 and first lit in 1769. Philadelphia's mariners had pressed for it: many ships had been lost in the waters around the cape, and the approach to the Delaware Bay needed a light. It was among the earliest lighthouses built in the colonies.

The Revolution

In 1777, during the American Revolution, the British nearly destroyed it. The wardens repaired the damage, and the light was burning again by 1784.

The sand

What the war could not finish, the shoreline did. By 1897 the dune around the tower was reported to be blowing away at three to five feet a year. In 1905 several tons of brush were laid around the tower and its oil house to keep the sand from drifting out from under the foundations and walls.

It was not enough. Shoreline erosion undermined the foundation, and the lighthouse was abandoned.

April 13, 1926

On April 13, 1926, the Cape Henlopen Lighthouse collapsed into the sea.

A state historical marker now tells its story. The lighthouse itself is gone, and so is the ground it stood on.

What the cape still says

Cape Henlopen is a moving landscape. The same park that lost its lighthouse to the sea is where The Point closes each spring for nesting shorebirds and reopens in the fall, and where the dunes are fenced and managed. The lighthouse is the clearest lesson in why: on this coast, the land does not stay where it is put.

Sources: U.S. Coast Guard Historian's Office, Cape Henlopen Lighthouse history (history.uscg.mil), for the 1767 completion and 1769 lighting, the mariners' petition, the 1777 damage and 1784 relighting, the erosion reports of 1897 and 1905, abandonment and the April 13, 1926 collapse; the Cape Henlopen Lighthouse historical marker (Historical Marker Database); the Cape Gazette's anniversary coverage of the collapse. The lighthouse's rank among colonial lighthouses differs across accounts and is described generally. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit the marker for this story.

stories.headline: The Day the British Shelled Lewes
stories.hook: On April 6 and 7, 1813, a British squadron bombarded Lewes. A cannonball is still lodged in the foundation of one of the houses it hit.
stories.lede: In the spring of 1813, the War of 1812 came to Lewes from the water.
stories.body:
In the spring of 1813, the War of 1812 came to Lewes from the water. On April 6 and 7, 1813, a British naval squadron bombarded the town.

The blockade

After the war began, British naval forces set up a partial blockade of the American coast and made sporadic attacks on coastal towns and shipping. Lewes, at the mouth of the Delaware Bay, was in their path. Over those two days of naval fire, numerous homes and businesses in town were damaged.

The Cannonball House

One of them is still standing, and still carries the evidence. The house now called the Cannonball House was built around 1765. It was once the home of Gilbert McCracken and David Rowland, pilots for the Bay and River Delaware, the men who guided ships through the bay. An iron cannonball from the bombardment is lodged in its foundation.

The Lewes Historical Society acquired the house in 1963 and made it a maritime museum. Its exhibits cover the War of 1812, the navigation of the Delaware Bay and River, and Lewes's own maritime story.

A state marker

On April 5, 2003, the State of Delaware honored the house with a historical marker for its association with the bombardment and as the home of two pilots of the Bay and River Delaware, Gilbert McCracken and his son Henry.

Seeing it

The Cannonball House was one of the landmarks tied to this month's Lewes Maritime Weekend, when the Boast the Coast festival offered free visits associated with it. Its regular hours and admission are set by the Lewes Historical Society; check the society's current information before you go.

It is an ordinary-looking colonial house, which is the point. The war did not come to Lewes as a battle on a field. It came as cannon fire into the houses of the people who lived there, and one of those houses kept the proof.

Sources: Delaware Public Archives historical marker for the Cannonball House (archives.delaware.gov) for the April 6–7, 1813 bombardment, the house's c. 1765 date, the McCracken and Rowland pilots, the cannonball in the foundation and the April 5, 2003 state recognition; the Lewes Historical Society's Cannonball House page (historiclewes.org) for its 1963 acquisition and museum exhibits; the British blockade context as described in those sources. Claims that the house is the only surviving damaged building are not consistently sourced and are omitted. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit for this story.

stories.headline: Two Lights on the Breakwaters
stories.hook: Off Cape Henlopen, two lighthouses stand on stone breakwaters built to make a harbor where there was none. Their story starts with an act of Congress in 1825.
stories.lede: Look out from Lewes Beach toward the mouth of the bay and you will see two lighthouses standing on lines of stone in the water.
stories.body:
Look out from the Lewes shore toward the mouth of the bay and two lighthouses stand on lines of stone in the water. They are the Delaware Breakwater East End Lighthouse and the Harbor of Refuge Lighthouse, and they exist because the mouth of the Delaware Bay had no natural harbor.

Making a harbor

In 1825 an act of Congress authorized a breakwater off Cape Henlopen, to create a harbor where ships could shelter in stormy weather. Building it took decades: the breakwater was not completed until 1869.

East End, 1885

The Delaware Breakwater East End Lighthouse was built in 1885 on the eastern end of that breakwater. It is a conical tower of cast iron plates lined with brick.

It was fitted with a fourth-order Fresnel lens showing a fixed white light, with a red sector facing the sea to warn mariners off the dangerous shoals of Cape Henlopen. It was automated on July 11, 1950, and decommissioned in 1996.

Harbor of Refuge, 1902 to 1926

A second, outer breakwater followed: the National Harbor of Refuge. A temporary light was set up on its south end on Jan. 1, 1902. A three-story frame lighthouse replaced it in 1908, but a series of storms damaged that structure, and it was removed and replaced in 1926.

Coast Guard keepers manned the Harbor of Refuge light until it was automated in December 1973.

Seeing them

Both lights are offshore, and neither is reached on foot. They are best seen from the Lewes and Cape Henlopen shore, where the lines of the breakwaters show how much stone it took to make the bay safe to wait in. Delaware State Parks has written about both as part of the southern coast's lighthouse history.

Sources: U.S. Coast Guard Historian's Office, Harbor of Refuge Lighthouse history (history.uscg.mil), for the 1825 authorization, the 1869 completion, the 1902 temporary light, the 1908 and 1926 structures and the December 1973 automation; the Delaware Breakwater East End Lighthouse historical marker (Historical Marker Database) for the 1885 construction, materials, lens, red sector, 1950 automation and 1996 decommissioning; Delaware State Parks' "Shining a Light on Delaware's Historic Southern Coast Lighthouses." Access to the lights is not described here. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit for this story.

stories.headline: A Dutch Town Hall in Lewes
stories.hook: The Zwaanendael Museum was built in 1931 for the 300th anniversary of Delaware's first European colony, and modeled on the town hall of Hoorn in the Netherlands.
stories.lede: The most unusual building in Lewes was designed to look like it belonged in Holland.
stories.body:
The most unusual building in Lewes was designed to look as if it belonged in Holland. That is exactly what it was meant to do.

A building for an anniversary

The Zwaanendael Museum was built in 1931 to mark the 300th anniversary of Swanendael, the state's first European colony. The Dutch settled it in 1631 along the Hoorn Kill, the waterway now called the Lewes-Rehoboth Canal.

Modeled on Hoorn

The building is modeled on the town hall in Hoorn, in the Netherlands. Its stepped facade gable, carved stonework and decorated shutters are the details that make it stand out on a Lewes street.

It was designed by E. William Martin, the architect of two of the state's most familiar buildings in Dover: Legislative Hall and the Hall of Records.

What it holds

The Zwaanendael is a museum of the Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs. It has been accredited by the American Alliance of Museums. Over the years its exhibits and programs have covered the Swanendael colony, the British warship DeBraak lost off the cape in 1798, and the wider history of the Lewes area. Its "Mysteries of History" walking tours explore the town's stranger stories.

Kept up

A building meant to look old has to be looked after. The Division carried out a rehabilitation of the museum's exterior beginning in 2020, to keep the details that define it in good condition.

Seeing it

The museum stands at 102 Kings Highway in Lewes. Hours and current exhibits are set by the Division; check its current listings before you go. Even from the street, it is one of the clearest reminders that Lewes's story begins with the Dutch, nearly a century before most of the town's colonial houses were built.

Sources: Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs, "Zwaanendael Museum History" (history.delaware.gov), for the 1931 construction, the 300th anniversary of Swanendael, the Hoorn Kill, the Hoorn town hall model, the facade details and the architect E. William Martin; the Division's 2018 note on American Alliance of Museums accreditation and its 2020 note on exterior rehabilitation; State of Delaware News on the museum's "Mysteries of History" tours. The comparison with the age of Lewes's colonial houses is general and not a dated claim. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit for this story.

stories.headline: The Light at the Bottom of Delaware
stories.hook: The Fenwick Island Lighthouse was lit in 1859 and shone for nearly 120 years. At its base is a stone that marked the Delaware–Maryland line in 1751.
stories.lede: At the southern edge of Delaware's coast, two very different markers share one small piece of ground.
stories.body:
At the southern edge of Delaware's coast, two very different markers share one small piece of ground: a lighthouse that guided ships for nearly 120 years, and a stone that helped settle where Delaware ends.

The lighthouse

The Fenwick Island Lighthouse was completed in 1858 to help mariners avoid the Fenwick Shoals, which lie about six miles off the coast. It stands 87 feet tall and is the only brick, conical-type lighthouse ever built in the state. A third-order Fresnel lens of French manufacture was installed, and the light was first turned on on Aug. 1, 1859.

It operated without interruption for nearly 120 years, until the U.S. Coast Guard decommissioned it on Dec. 13, 1978.

Saved, and relit

A grassroots effort followed. Ownership of the property was transferred to the State of Delaware in 1981, and in 1982 the lighthouse was relit as an unofficial, private aid to navigation. The Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs manages the complex and leases it to the New Friends of the Fenwick Island Lighthouse. In 2025 the 1858 lightkeeper's house also came under the Division's care.

The stone

On the lighthouse grounds is the Transpeninsular Line marker, erected on April 26, 1751. It marks the eastern end of a line surveyed by John Watson and William Parsons of Pennsylvania and John Emory and Thomas Jones of Maryland. The line set the east–west boundary between Pennsylvania's three lower counties, now Delaware, and the colony of Maryland, and fixed the middle point of the peninsula 35 miles to the west.

It is one of the oldest boundary markers on the coast, and it explains a good deal about the shape of the state.

Seeing it

The lighthouse has been undergoing renovation in recent years, and its open days and hours are set by the Division and the Friends. Check their current information before you plan a visit.

Sources: Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs, "History was made here: Fenwick Island Lighthouse" (history.delaware.gov), for the 1858 construction, the Fenwick Shoals, the 87-foot height, the only brick conical lighthouse in the state, the lens and the Aug. 1, 1859 lighting, the Dec. 13, 1978 decommissioning and the Transpeninsular Line marker; the Division's 2024 update and 2025 note for the 1981 state ownership, the 1982 relighting, the lease to the New Friends of the Fenwick Island Lighthouse and the lightkeeper's house; the U.S. Coast Guard Historian's Office's Fenwick Island Lighthouse history. "One of the oldest boundary markers on the coast" is a general description, not a ranked claim. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit for this story.

stories.headline: Bethany Beach at 125
stories.hook: Bethany Beach was founded in July 1901 as a church seaside retreat and incorporated in 1909. This year the town marked its 125th summer.
stories.lede: Bethany Beach began as an idea about what a summer by the sea was for.
stories.body:
Bethany Beach began as an idea about what a summer by the sea was for. This year the town marked its 125th anniversary.

A retreat, by design

Bethany's founding has its roots in the Disciples of Christ church and its Christian Missionary Society. Looking for a seaside community for summer retreats and educational programs, the church formed a committee to find a site on the Delmarva coast. Bethany Beach was founded in July 1901, at the start of its first summer season.

The town was not formally incorporated until 1909.

The Tabernacle

At the center of the new town was an octagonal auditorium called the Tabernacle, built in 1901. For six decades it was Bethany's meeting place, hosting church gatherings and town events, until it was torn down in 1961 and replaced.

125 years on

The town marked the anniversary through the summer. Founders Day Weekend, over Labor Day weekend from Sept. 4 to 7, celebrated Bethany's 125th birthday alongside the nation's 250th. In September the town and its Cultural Affairs Committee held "A Passport to the Past" at the Dinker-Irvin Museum, guiding visitors through six areas of the town's history.

What lasted

A lot has changed since the Tabernacle. What has lasted is the town's sense of what it is for: a quieter beach, built around families and summers, more than nightlife. The founders were looking for a retreat. A century and a quarter later, that is still the word most people reach for.

Sources: The Town of Bethany Beach's Spring 2026 newsletter (townofbethanybeach.com) and Coastal Point's report on the Founders Day celebrations for the founding, the 125th anniversary and Founders Day Weekend; Delaware Public Media's "Bethany Beach to celebrate 125 years" for the Dinker-Irvin Museum event; Best of Bethany's town history for the Disciples of Christ, the 1909 incorporation and the Tabernacle. The closing characterization of the town is the publication's own. Delaware Beach Finds did not attend the anniversary events.
